In finite game trees with perfect information, backward induction solves from the end:

title: Dynamic reasoning
text:
One-step backward induction






NoteBackward induction steps



Step 1 (Player 2):
After \(A\): compare \((2,1)\) vs \((0,0)\) → choose L (since \(1>0\)).
After \(B\): compare \((1,2)\) vs \((3,0)\) → choose L (since \(2>0\)).
Step 2 (Player 1):
If \(A\) → payoff \(2\).
If \(B\) → payoff \(1\).
So choose A.
Outcome: \((A,L)\).

Bellman idea (optional, for dynamic optimization)
Dynamic programming often writes:
\[
V(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\bigl\{ r(s,a) + \beta V(s') \bigr\}.
\]
Same “optimize now + value of continuation” logic.

title: Optimization
text:
A best response is an optimization problem. Given others’ strategies \(s_{-i}\), player \(i\) chooses
\[
BR_i(s_{-i})\in \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
Intuition. A Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of best responses: everyone is already choosing an argmax given others.

title: Optimization
text:
A best response is an optimization problem. Given others’ strategies \(s_{-i}\), player \(i\) chooses
\[

\]
Intuition. A Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of best responses: everyone is already choosing an argmax given others.

title: Optimization
text:
FOC / SOC (unconstrained)
If \(f\) is differentiable and you maximize over an interval, an interior optimum \(x^*\) satisfies the first-order condition (FOC)
\[
f'(x^*)=0.
\]
If \(f\) is twice differentiable, the second-order condition (SOC) for a local maximum is
\[
f''(x^*)<0.
\]
Intuition. FOC finds stationary points; SOC checks that the curve bends downward.

title: Optimization
text:
KKT conditions (constrained)
For maximizing \(f(x)\) subject to inequality constraints \(g_j(x)\le 0\), define the Lagrangian
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\sum_{j}\lambda_j g_j(x),
\qquad \lambda_j\ge 0.
\]
KKT conditions (at an optimum, under standard regularity assumptions) include: - Stationarity: \(\nabla_x \mathcal{L}(x^*,\lambda^*)=0\) - Primal feasibility: \(g_j(x^*)\le 0\) - Dual feasibility: \(\lambda_j^*\ge 0\) - Complementary slackness: \(\lambda_j^* g_j(x^*)=0\) for all \(j\)
Intuition. Constraints either bind (then they get a positive “shadow price” \(\lambda_j\)) or don’t bind (then \(\lambda_j=0\)).

title: Optimization
section: Example: best response with a constraint
text:
Example: best response with a constraint
Maximize \(f(x)=2x-x^2\) subject to \(x\ge 0\).
Write the constraint as \(g(x)=-x\le 0\). Lagrangian:
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)= (2x-x^2)-\lambda(-x)=2x-x^2+\lambda x.
\]
KKT: - Stationarity: \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=2-2x+\lambda=0\) - Primal feasibility: \(x\ge 0\) - Dual feasibility: \(\lambda\ge 0\) - Complementary slackness: \(\lambda x=0\)
From stationarity: \(2-2x+\lambda=0 \Rightarrow x=1+\lambda/2\).
If \(x>0\), then complementary slackness implies \(\lambda=0\), so \(x=1\). Check feasibility: \(1\ge 0\) yes. So the solution is \(x^*=1\).
(If the unconstrained maximizer had been negative, the constraint would bind and you’d get \(x^*=0\) with \(\lambda>0\).)

title: Probability
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over actions. If the action set is finite, this is just a probability vector (see the simplex definition in Linear algebra).
Intuition. “Randomizing” in game theory is not mystical: it’s a distribution that other players can form beliefs about.

title: Probability
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over actions. If the action set is finite, this is just a probability vector (see the simplex definition in Linear algebra).

title: Probability
text:
Expectation
If a random variable \(X\) takes values \(x_k\) with probabilities \(p_k\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_k x_k p_k.
\]
In games, expected utility under a mixed strategy is exactly this idea: average the payoff over all possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.

title: Probability
text:
Bayes’ rule
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\,\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}.
\]
Intuition. Prior belief \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) gets updated by how well \(A\) predicts the evidence \(B\).

title: Probability
text:
Example: updating beliefs about types
A player is either type \(H\) or \(L\). Prior \(\mathbb{P}(H)=0.3\), \(\mathbb{P}(L)=0.7\). You observe a signal \(s\). Suppose
\[
\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)=0.8,\qquad \mathbb{P}(s\mid L)=0.2.
\]
First compute the overall likelihood of \(s\):
\[
\mathbb{P}(s)=\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)\mathbb{P}(H)+\mathbb{P}(s\mid L)\mathbb{P}(L)=0.8\cdot 0.3+0.2\cdot 0.7=0.38.
\]
Then the posterior belief is
\[
\mathbb{P}(H\mid s)=\frac{0.8\cdot 0.3}{0.38}\approx 0.6316.
\]
So after observing \(s\), belief in type \(H\) rises from \(0.3\) to about \(0.63\).

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
A fixed point of a function \(f:X\to X\) is a point \(x^*\) such that \[
f(x^*)=x^*.
\]
Intuition. An equilibrium is often a fixed point: if “best response” maps strategies into strategies, equilibrium is where nothing changes.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
A fixed point of a function \(f:X\to X\) is a point \(x^*\) such that \[
f(x^*)=x^*.
\]
Intuition. An equilibrium is often a fixed point: if “best response” maps strategies into strategies, equilibrium is where nothing changes.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Brouwer (idea)
Brouwer’s fixed point theorem (informal): a continuous function from a compact convex set to itself has a fixed point.
This supports existence of equilibrium in many continuous games.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Correspondences (set-valued maps)
A correspondence \(F:X \rightrightarrows X\) assigns a set \(F(x)\) to each \(x\). Best responses are usually correspondences: \[
BR_i(s_{-i}) = \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}),
\] which may contain multiple maximizers.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Kakutani (idea)
Kakutani’s theorem (informal): under continuity-like conditions and nonempty convex values, a correspondence has a fixed point: \[
x^* \in F(x^*).
\]
This is the classic route to Nash existence with mixed strategies: the product of best-response correspondences has a fixed point.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Example: fixed point intuition in 1D
Let \(f(x)=\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{4}\) on \([0,1]\). Solve \(x=f(x)\): \[
x=\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{4}\Rightarrow x^*=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Equilibrium-as-fixed-point is exactly this: apply the rule, you land back on yourself.

title: Linear algebra
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability vector over pure actions. If player \(i\) has \(m\) pure actions, a mixed strategy is
\[
\Delta^{m-1}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m:\; x_k\ge 0\;\forall k,\;\sum_{k=1}^m x_k = 1\right\},
\]
the \((m-1)\)-simplex.
Intuition. You can think of \(x\) as a “weighting” of actions. The simplex condition just says: nonnegative weights that sum to 1.

title: Linear algebra
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability vector over pure actions. If player \(i\) has \(m\) pure actions, a mixed strategy is
\[
\Delta^{m-1}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m:\; x_k\ge 0\;\forall k,\;\sum_{k=1}^m x_k = 1\right\},

title: Linear algebra
text:
Payoff matrices and expected payoff
In a two-player normal-form game, let player 1 have \(m\) actions and player 2 have \(n\) actions. Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be player 1’s payoff matrix (and \(B\) for player 2). If player 1 plays \(x\in\Delta^{m-1}\) and player 2 plays \(y\in\Delta^{n-1}\), then player 1’s expected payoff is
\[
u_1(x,y)=x^\top A y.
\]
Intuition. First compute expected payoffs against each of player 2’s pure actions (\(Ay\)). Then average those numbers using player 1’s mixing weights (\(x^\top\)).

title: Linear algebra
text:
Example: 2×2 game
Suppose
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 0\\
1 & 3
\end{pmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{pmatrix}0.4\\0.6\end{pmatrix},\quad
y=\begin{pmatrix}0.25\\0.75\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Compute
\[
Ay=
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 0\\
1 & 3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0.25\\0.75
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.5\\
2.5
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
u_1(x,y)=x^\top(Ay)=0.4\cdot 0.5+0.6\cdot 2.5=1.7.
\]
So the mixed-vs-mixed expected payoff is \(1.7\) for player 1.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
In Bayesian and information economics, “information” is usually represented by what events a player can distinguish.
There are two common (equivalent) ways to think about it:

Information partition (finite case): a player observes which cell of a partition they are in.
\(\sigma\)-algebra (general case): the collection of events the player can condition on.

You almost never need heavy measure theory for standard game theory notes—just the intuition.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
In Bayesian and information economics, “information” is usually represented by what events a player can distinguish.
There are two common (equivalent) ways to think about it:

Information partition (finite case): a player observes which cell of a partition they are in.
\(\sigma\)-algebra (general case): the collection of events the player can condition on.

You almost never need heavy measure theory for standard game theory notes—just the intuition.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
\(\sigma\)-algebra (concept only)
Let \(\Omega\) be the set of possible states of the world.
A \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) is a collection of subsets of \(\Omega\) (events) such that:

\(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\)

If \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) then \(A^c \in \mathcal{F}\)

If \(A_1, A_2, \dots \in \mathcal{F}\) then \(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty A_k \in \mathcal{F}\)

Intuition. \(\mathcal{F}\) lists the events you are able to talk about (and condition on).
Coarser \(\mathcal{F}\) = less information.

Finite shortcut (partition view)
If \(\Omega\) is finite and a player’s information is a partition \[
\Pi = \{C_1,\dots,C_m\},
\] then the player can distinguish only which cell \(C_j\) contains the true state.
The corresponding \(\sigma\)-algebra is “all unions of cells of \(\Pi\)”.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
section: Conditional expectation as “best prediction given information”
text:
Conditional expectation as “best prediction given information”
Given an integrable random variable \(X\) (e.g., payoff-relevant quantity) and an information set \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) is the random variable that represents the best mean-squared prediction of \(X\) using only information in \(\mathcal{G}\).
Projection idea (intuition). Think of \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) as projecting \(X\) onto the space of \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable variables (things you can compute using the information you have).

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
section: Example: conditional expectation with a partition
text:
Example: conditional expectation with a partition
Let the state space be \[
\Omega=\{\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4\},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(\omega_k)=\tfrac14 \text{ for each }k.
\]
Let \[
X(\omega_1)=0,\;X(\omega_2)=2,\;X(\omega_3)=4,\;X(\omega_4)=6.
\]
Suppose the player only observes whether the state is in \[
C_1=\{\omega_1,\omega_2\}\quad\text{or}\quad C_2=\{\omega_3,\omega_4\}.
\]
That information corresponds to a partition \(\Pi=\{C_1,C_2\}\) (and a \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by it).
Then the conditional expectation is constant on each cell:

On \(C_1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid C_1]
=\frac{X(\omega_1)+X(\omega_2)}{2}
=\frac{0+2}{2}=1.
\]
On \(C_2\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid C_2]
=\frac{X(\omega_3)+X(\omega_4)}{2}
=\frac{4+6}{2}=5.
\]

So \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) takes value \(1\) if you learn “cell \(C_1\)”, and value \(5\) if you learn “cell \(C_2\)”.
Game theory interpretation. This is exactly what beliefs do: you map what you observed to an updated expectation of payoff-relevant quantities.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
Common knowledge (concept)
An event \(E\) is common knowledge if: - everyone knows \(E\), - everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), - everyone knows that everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), - and so on indefinitely.
Intuition. Common knowledge is what makes coordination possible (or impossible). It is stronger than “everyone knows”.

Iterated beliefs (one-line idea)
In Bayesian games, strategies can depend on: - beliefs about types, - beliefs about others’ beliefs, - higher-order beliefs.
Often you don’t compute these explicitly; you just need to know they exist and that equilibrium concepts impose consistency.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
Practical takeaway
For most game theory work: - partitions are enough to model information, - conditional expectation captures “best prediction given what you know”, - common knowledge / higher-order beliefs matter conceptually for coordination and equilibrium.

title: Convexity & concavity
text:
A set \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if for any \(x,y\in C\) and any \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[
\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y \in C.
\]
Intuition. If you can take “mixtures” of two feasible points and stay feasible, the set is convex. This is exactly why mixed strategies live in a simplex.

title: Convexity & concavity
text:
A set \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if for any \(x,y\in C\) and any \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[
\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y \in C.
\]
Intuition. If you can take “mixtures” of two feasible points and stay feasible, the set is convex. This is exactly why mixed strategies live in a simplex.

title: Convexity & concavity
text:
Concave functions
A function \(f\) is concave on a convex set if for any \(x,y\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[
f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y)\ge \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda)f(y).
\]
Intuition. Concavity means “diminishing returns” and makes optimization well-behaved: local maxima are global.

title: Convexity & concavity
section: Example: why concavity helps best responses
text:
Example: why concavity helps best responses
Let \(f(x)=2x-x^2\) on \([0,2]\). Then \(f''(x)=-2<0\), so \(f\) is concave and the maximizer is unique.
FOC: \(f'(x)=2-2x=0 \Rightarrow x^*=1\).
In games, concavity in your own action often implies a unique best response.
